interactions.label: Which of the following best defines somatic (clinical) death?

params.question: Which of the following best defines somatic (clinical) death?

answers.text: Sequential death of individual cells, beginning with neurons and ending with skeletal muscle

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This describes cellular (molecular) death, which follows somatic death and occurs in a tissue-dependent sequence — neurons die first, skeletal muscle cells last.

answers.text: Irreversible cessation of the integrated vital functions — heartbeat, respiration, and CNS activity

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Somatic death is defined as the permanent, irreversible cessation of the three integrated vital functions of the organism as a whole.

answers.text: Permanent cessation of electrical activity in the cerebral cortex alone

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Isolated loss of cortical activity describes cortical death. Somatic death requires cessation of all integrated vital functions, not just cortical electrical activity.

answers.text: Any cessation of heartbeat, regardless of whether resuscitation is possible

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The defining criterion is irreversibility. Brief cardiorespiratory arrest followed by successful CPR does not constitute somatic death — the reversibility window has not yet closed.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the distinction: somatic death = irreversible loss of integrated vital functions (heartbeat, respiration, CNS). The key word is 'irreversible' — if CPR can restore function, somatic death has not occurred.
Somatic death is irreversible cessation of all integrated vital functions. The brief reversibility window after apparent arrest is the clinical basis for CPR and defibrillation.

params.question: Among adults, approximately 70–80% of sudden unexpected natural deaths are attributed to which organ system?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: CNS causes such as subarachnoid haemorrhage and epilepsy contribute to sudden death, but they account for a much smaller proportion than cardiovascular causes.
Respiratory causes (e.g., massive pulmonary embolism, status asthmaticus) are recognised but account for a smaller proportion than cardiovascular disease.
Correct. Approximately 70–80% of sudden natural deaths in adults are cardiovascular in origin, with ischaemic heart disease (IHD) being the single most common cause.
GI causes of sudden death (e.g., massive variceal haemorrhage, acute pancreatitis) are uncommon relative to the cardiovascular system's dominant contribution.

overallFeedback.feedback: In adults, 70–80% of sudden unexpected natural deaths are cardiovascular in origin. IHD (ischaemic heart disease) is the single most common cause — a high-yield forensic fact.

The cardiovascular system — particularly ischaemic heart disease — is overwhelmingly the leading cause of sudden natural death in adults, which is why autopsy protocols prioritise coronary artery examination.

interactions.label: Why is the standard cooling rate of approximately 1.5°C per hour in algor mortis

params.question: Why is the standard cooling rate of approximately 1.5°C per hour in algor mortis considered only a rough guide for estimating the post-mortem interval?

answers.text: Because rigor mortis generates metabolic heat that raises the core temperature after death

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Rigor mortis involves ATP depletion and actin-myosin cross-linking but does not generate significant heat. The variability in cooling rate is due to environmental and body-related factors.

answers.text: Because autopsy thermometers are inherently imprecise at low body temperatures

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Modern forensic thermometers are sufficiently precise. The variability arises from biological and environmental factors — body size, insulation, ambient temperature — not from measurement error.

answers.text: Because post-mortem lividity redistributes warm blood to the surface, artificially raising skin temperature

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Lividity is passive gravitational pooling of blood in dependent areas — it does not actively redistribute warm blood or meaningfully affect the rate of core temperature decline.

answers.text: Because the actual rate is modified by ambient temperature, body habitus, clothing, and environmental exposure

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The 1.5°C/hr figure assumes standard conditions (exposed body, ambient ~20–22°C). In practice, obese bodies cool more slowly, clothed bodies retain heat longer, and ambient temperature extremes significantly alter the rate.

overallFeedback.feedback: The standard cooling rate varies because multiple factors affect heat loss: ambient temperature, body weight and habitus (obese bodies cool more slowly), clothing and coverings, and whether the body is indoors or outdoors.
The 1.5°C/hr figure is a useful starting estimate, but always consider body habitus, clothing, ambient temperature, and environmental exposure when estimating PMI from algor mortis.

interactions.label: If post-mortem lividity is fixed on the back and buttocks but the body is discov

params.question: If post-mortem lividity is fixed on the back and buttocks but the body is discovered in a prone (face-down) position, this indicates the body was moved after lividity became fixed.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is true. Lividity fixes in the dependent parts where blood pooled under gravity. If fixed lividity is posterior but the body is found prone, the body must have been moved after fixation — this discrepancy is a key forensic indicator that the death scene may have been altered.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. Fixed lividity reflects the position in which the body lay during the fixation period. A mismatch between the distribution of fixed lividity and the body's position at discovery is strong evidence of post-mortem repositioning — a finding of significant medicolegal importance.
